cards.title: Espresso
cards.definition: Espresso is a concentrated coffee beverage brewed by forcing hot water through finely ground coffee under pressure.
cards.why: Nearly every café drink begins with espresso.
cards.tip: Master consistency before chasing perfection.
cards.mistake: Judging espresso by crema alone.
cards.challenge: Explain espresso in one sentence.

cards.title: Extraction
cards.definition: The removal of soluble compounds from coffee using water.
cards.why: Extraction determines sweetness, acidity and bitterness.
cards.tip: Taste every shot.
cards.mistake: Relying on shot time alone.
cards.challenge: Describe over-extraction.

cards.title: Latte Art
cards.definition: Latte art combines espresso, milk texture and pouring technique.
cards.why: Good latte art is evidence of good milk preparation.
cards.tip: Perfect texture before learning advanced patterns.
cards.mistake: Focusing on patterns instead of milk quality.
cards.challenge: Name three classic latte art designs.

cards.title: Filter Coffee
cards.definition: Filter coffee is brewed by allowing gravity to draw water through a bed of ground coffee.
cards.why: It highlights clarity, sweetness and origin character more than espresso.
cards.tip: Focus on even extraction rather than speed.
cards.mistake: Grinding too fine.
cards.challenge: List three differences between espresso and filter coffee.

cards.title: Espresso Machine
cards.definition: An espresso machine forces hot water through finely ground coffee under controlled pressure and temperature.
cards.why: It is the heart of most specialty coffee bars.
cards.tip: Allow the machine to fully warm before service.
cards.mistake: Assuming a machine is stable immediately after switching on.
cards.challenge: Why is thermal stability important?

cards.title: Workflow
cards.definition: Workflow is the sequence of actions used to prepare drinks efficiently and consistently.
cards.why: Good workflow reduces mistakes, waste and customer wait times.
cards.tip: Move with purpose rather than speed.
cards.mistake: Crossing over your own workspace.
cards.challenge: List three ways to improve workflow during a busy service.

cards.title: Sensory Evaluation
cards.definition: Sensory evaluation is the systematic assessment of coffee using sight, aroma, taste and mouthfeel.
cards.why: Consistent sensory skills improve quality control and buying decisions.
cards.tip: Taste with purpose, not just preference.
cards.mistake: Confusing personal preference with objective quality.
cards.challenge: List the five senses involved in coffee evaluation.

cards.title: Green Coffee
cards.definition: Green coffee is coffee that has been processed, dried and prepared for export before roasting.
cards.why: Every flavour in roasted coffee begins with green coffee quality.
cards.tip: Inspect green coffee before roasting.
cards.mistake: Judging quality from origin alone.
cards.challenge: What characteristics define high-quality green coffee?

cards.title: Coffee Processing
cards.definition: Processing is the method used to remove the coffee seed from the fruit after harvesting.
cards.why: Processing has a major influence on flavour, body and acidity.
cards.tip: Always consider processing alongside origin and variety.
cards.mistake: Assuming origin alone determines flavour.
cards.challenge: Name the three most common processing methods.

cards.title: Coffee Origin
cards.definition: Origin refers to the country or region where coffee is grown.
cards.why: Climate, altitude, soil and processing all influence flavour.
cards.tip: Think of origin as one part of a coffee's story.
cards.mistake: Assuming every coffee from one country tastes the same.
cards.challenge: Name three major coffee-producing countries.

cards.title: First Crack
cards.definition: First crack occurs when internal pressure causes the bean structure to fracture audibly.
cards.why: It marks the beginning of development.
cards.tip: Listen as well as watch your data.
cards.mistake: Treating first crack as the finish line.
cards.challenge: Why does first crack occur?

cards.title: Coffee Value
cards.definition: Coffee value is the combination of product quality, service, experience and trust perceived by the customer.
cards.why: Customers judge value by the complete experience rather than ingredient cost alone.
cards.tip: Compete on experience and consistency, not simply price.
cards.mistake: Assuming cheaper automatically means better value.
cards.challenge: Describe what makes a €4 coffee feel worth €4.

cards.title: Pour-Over (V60)
cards.definition: Pour-over brewing using a conical single-hole filter (like the Hario V60) where the brewer controls extraction through pour rate, agitation and timing.
cards.why: Because the flow rate is entirely manual, it gives the brewer more real-time control over extraction than almost any other method.
cards.tip: Keep your pour steady and consistent rather than fast or slow — repeatability matters more than speed.
cards.mistake: Pouring too fast and flooding the bed, which drowns out manual control entirely.
cards.challenge: What happens to extraction if you pour in one continuous stream versus several pulses?

cards.title: Panama: Boquete and the Geisha Boom
cards.definition: A high-altitude Panamanian region that became world-famous after Hacienda La Esmeralda's Geisha variety won Best of Panama in 2004, redefining what buyers would pay for exceptional coffee.
cards.why: It single-handedly changed the ceiling on coffee auction prices and put an entire variety on the map worldwide.
cards.tip: Geisha from Boquete tends toward intense jasmine, bergamot and tropical fruit — taste it once to understand the hype.
cards.mistake: Assuming every Geisha-labeled coffee will deliver Esmeralda-level quality just because of the variety name.
cards.challenge: What does the Boquete story reveal about how much variety and terroir can outweigh processing alone?

cards.title: Gesha (Geisha)
cards.definition: A variety originally from Ethiopia that became world-famous after a Panamanian lot won Best of Panama in 2004, prized for intense jasmine, bergamot and tropical fruit character.
cards.why: It redefined how much buyers would pay for exceptional coffee and put a single variety name on menus worldwide.
cards.tip: Yields are typically low and the plant is delicate — part of why Gesha commands such high prices.
cards.mistake: Assuming every coffee labeled Gesha will deliver the same intensity — growing conditions matter enormously for this variety.
cards.challenge: Why might the same variety produce a legendary cup in Panama but a merely average one elsewhere?

cards.title: The Physics of Foam Stability
cards.definition: Stable milk foam depends on a thin protein film forming around trapped air bubbles, while fat works to destabilize that same structure over time.
cards.why: Understanding this tension between protein and fat explains almost every practical foam problem baristas encounter.
cards.tip: If foam looks great immediately but collapses fast, suspect fat interference or insufficient protein structure, not just air volume.
cards.mistake: Judging foam quality only in the moment it's poured, without considering how it holds up over the next minute.
cards.challenge: Why does foam that looks identical right after steaming sometimes collapse at very different rates?

cards.title: TDS and Refractometry
cards.definition: Total Dissolved Solids (TDS) measures the concentration of dissolved coffee compounds in a brew, typically read using a refractometer.
cards.why: TDS gives an objective number for strength, replacing guesswork with a measurement that's directly comparable across brews.
cards.tip: A refractometer reads TDS in seconds, but always combine it with tasting — the number alone doesn't tell you if a brew tastes good.
cards.mistake: Treating a 'correct' TDS number as proof of quality without actually tasting the coffee.
cards.challenge: Why do a refractometer's TDS reading and extraction yield need to be calculated together, not read independently?

cards.title: Supertasters and Non-Tasters
cards.definition: Genetic variation in taste bud density means some people (supertasters) perceive bitterness and intensity far more strongly than others (non-tasters), with most people falling somewhere in between.
cards.why: This is a big part of why palates genuinely differ between people, not just a matter of experience or training.
cards.tip: When calibrating as a team, remember that a colleague's different palate sensitivity isn't necessarily wrong — it may be genuinely biological.
cards.mistake: Assuming everyone's baseline sensitivity to bitterness or intensity starts from the same place.
cards.challenge: Why might a supertaster and a non-taster genuinely disagree about whether the same coffee is 'too bitter'?

cards.title: The Flavor Wheel
cards.definition: A standardized visual lexicon of flavor and aroma descriptors, developed to give tasters a shared vocabulary for communicating what they perceive.
cards.why: Without shared vocabulary, two tasters can perceive the same thing but describe it so differently that they seem to disagree when they actually don't.
cards.tip: Use the wheel to narrow from broad categories toward more specific descriptors, rather than guessing a specific note first.
cards.mistake: Treating flavor wheel terms as the only correct way to describe a sensation, rather than as a shared communication tool.
cards.challenge: Why might two tasters use completely different words for the same underlying sensation without either being wrong?

cards.title: The Kaldi Legend
cards.definition: A popular origin story crediting an Ethiopian goat herder named Kaldi with discovering coffee after noticing his goats became energetic from eating certain red berries.
cards.why: It's the most widely told coffee origin story, even though it wasn't written down until centuries after it supposedly happened.
cards.tip: Treat Kaldi as folklore, not history — useful for context, not for citing as fact.
cards.mistake: Presenting the Kaldi legend as verified historical fact rather than a popular oral tradition.
cards.challenge: Why might a story like this survive for centuries even without historical evidence?

cards.title: Coffee in the Ottoman Empire
cards.definition: Coffee spread from Yemen into the Ottoman Empire by the 16th century, where dedicated coffeehouses called 'kiva han' became central to public life in cities like Istanbul.
cards.why: This is where coffee first became a genuine social institution, not just a drink — the coffeehouse as a public gathering space starts here.
cards.tip: Notice how quickly coffee moved from a private, medicinal drink to a public, social one once it reached Ottoman cities.
cards.mistake: Assuming coffee culture began in Europe rather than centuries earlier in the Ottoman world.
cards.challenge: Why might rulers have occasionally viewed coffeehouses with suspicion or tried to ban them?

cards.title: The Ethiopian Coffee Ceremony
cards.definition: A traditional, multi-hour ritual in Ethiopia where green beans are roasted, ground, and brewed fresh in front of guests in a clay pot called a jebena, usually performed by a woman of the household.
cards.why: Coffee originated in Ethiopia, and the ceremony remains the clearest living link between coffee's roots and how it's still consumed as a social, unhurried ritual rather than a quick transaction.
cards.tip: If you ever attend one, expect three rounds of coffee (abol, tona, baraka) — leaving after the first round is considered impolite.
cards.mistake: Assuming the ceremony is just 'how Ethiopians make coffee' rather than a deliberate social occasion, often reserved for guests, celebrations, or daily community bonding.
cards.challenge: Why might a culture build an hours-long ritual around a drink that takes minutes to brew elsewhere?

cards.title: Turkish Coffee and Fortune-Telling
cards.definition: Finely ground coffee simmered unfiltered in a small pot called a cezve, served with the grounds still in the cup — traditionally followed by reading patterns left in the sediment to tell fortunes.
cards.why: It's one of the oldest brewing methods still practiced today, and the fortune-telling tradition (tasseography) turned drinking coffee into a shared social and cultural performance.
cards.tip: Let the cup cool, flip it onto its saucer, and wait a few minutes before 'reading' the grounds — the shapes only form once the liquid has fully drained.
cards.mistake: Stirring or drinking the coffee to the very bottom — the thick sediment at the base isn't meant to be consumed.
cards.challenge: Why might a brewing method built around leftover sediment become a cherished tradition instead of a flaw to fix?

cards.title: The Staling Enemies: Oxygen, Light, Moisture, Heat
cards.definition: The four environmental factors that degrade roasted coffee fastest: oxygen oxidizes aromatic oils, light breaks down compounds through photodegradation, moisture accelerates staling reactions, and heat speeds up all of the above.
cards.why: Nearly every packaging and storage decision in coffee — valve bags, opaque packaging, airtight canisters, cool storage — exists specifically to block one or more of these four factors.
cards.tip: Rank them by how fast they act: oxygen and light do damage in hours to days, moisture and heat compound everything else, so a bag that blocks all four beats one that only blocks one or two.
cards.mistake: Focusing on just one factor (like buying an airtight canister) while ignoring the others — a canister on a sunny counter still lets light and heat do damage.
cards.challenge: Why might coffee packaging need to defend against four different threats instead of just sealing out air?

cards.title: V60 Pour-Over
cards.definition: A manual pour-over method using a cone-shaped dripper with a large single hole and spiral ribs, designed to give the brewer full control over pour rate and agitation.
cards.why: The V60 is one of the most widely used pour-over methods in specialty coffee, prized for producing a clean, bright cup that highlights a coffee's origin character.
cards.tip: Pour in slow, controlled circles rather than a single dump — consistent pour technique matters more to the final cup than almost any other variable in this method.
cards.mistake: Pouring too fast or unevenly, which causes channeling — water finding an easy path through the grounds instead of extracting evenly.
cards.challenge: Why might a dripper with only one large hole require more pouring skill than one with many small holes?

steps.title: Rinse the filter
steps.content: Rinse the paper filter with hot water to remove papery taste and preheat the dripper and vessel. Discard the rinse water.

steps.title: Add coffee, level, and bloom
steps.content: Add the ground coffee and level the bed. Start your timer and pour 40g of water, saturating all the grounds evenly. Let it bloom.

steps.title: First pour
steps.content: Pour to 160g total in slow, steady circles, keeping the water level fairly consistent.

steps.title: Second pour
steps.content: Pour the remaining water to reach 320g total, again in slow circles.

steps.title: Drawdown
steps.content: Let the water fully drain through. Total brew time should land around 2:30-3:00.

dial_in.fix: Grind finer, or raise the water temperature slightly.
Grind coarser, or pour a bit faster with fewer stages.

dial_in.issue: Drawdown stalls or runs very slow
dial_in.fix: Grind coarser — a stalled bed usually means the grind is too fine for this method.
